Many years ago I came to know a beggar. He was one of those beggars who have
no legs and push themselves around on a little platform with wheels, lue favorite spot
for him to practice his profession was the entrance to the subway where over 500,U00
people passed between the hours ol four and six o'clock in the evening. There he sta
tioned himself six days a week.
One day 1 had the temerity to ask him why he bothered to beg rather than take ad
vantage ot Uncle Sam's willingness to teach him a good trade. His answer was one that
1 shall never forget. It took the form of a few questions for which 1 found it easy to
supply the answers. He started out by saying, "Do you know how many people go
down these steps between four and six o'clocK?" 1 gave the answer, "Over 500,000,"
because 1 happened to know that fact. Then he said, "Suppose every one of those peo
ple dropped a penny in my hat, how much would 1 have after two hours?" That was
easy. My answer was $5,000.00. Then he came back with this. "Then suppose every
tenth person dropped a penny in the hat, what would I be making?" My answer was
$500.00.
Having gone through this interview I was weU aware of the reason why this haU of
a man was at the same spot six days a week between the hours of four and six o'clock.
He was sure of earning at least $3,000.00 in a week. And this was at a time when
skUled, union-protected labor had not yet reached the $5.00 an hour which Henry
Ford instituted much to the chagrin of his rival automobile makers of the time.
Much more recently, since I have been privUeged to contribute these diatiibes to
The Diamond, I have also come in contact frequently with the office of the Executive
Vice President, and others who are in charge of the destinies of our fraternity. One
fact I have discovered is that it costs more to operate our fraternity than our Alumni
Brothers have been donating each year. I also learned that a few wealthy members
had provided a modest endowment for the Executive CouncU. This reserve, however, is
being eroded by year to year operating deficits incurred even after the most frugal con
duct of affairs. I also became aware of the fact that there are over 17,000 Brothers in
Psi Upsilon who receive The Diamond.
That last bit of information brought me back to my beggar friend. When I first be
came acquainted with the size of our Alumni Brotherhood I kept turning back to those
questions of this beggar and the natural answers.
For instance, let us assume that every Alumnus Brother of Psi UpsUon could spare
ten dollars that he could dispatch to our headquarters. If every one did just that the
fraternity would be richer by $170,000. Such a sum would take care of expenses for
two years, or for one year and the balance could be retumed to the endowment ac
count.
Now the parable (U that is what it is) takes one further step. Suppose that each
Alumnus Brother should send along twenty dollars. That, naturally would double the
"kitty" and could start a precedent. There is no question about the fact that our fra
temity shaies the honor and distinction of being one of the very best. There is no doubt
that the several Chapters of the fraternity are situated in colleges and universities of
considerable distinction. There is a
great feeling among educational circles that a Psi
Upsilon Chapter is a credit in every way to the campus where it is located. It is also
accepted that the type of young men attracted to its membership are above average.
Last year 1,390 Brothers in Psi Upsilon contributed $36,960 to its coffers. That is an
average of $26.59 per contributor. This tells me that the $20 suggested above is not
beyond the realm of reason and is within the capability of our 17,000 alumni members.
And before I close I must pay my respects to my Uttle beggar for stirring my recol
lections and this treatise on the subject of giving to an organization which stUl con
tinues to produce gentlemen and scholars, just as it did in the days when he who reads
this was a part of the active entity of Psi Upsilon. Incidentally the Uttle beggar at his
death left an estate of $750,000.

Of the Executive Council
what probably must be recorded as a most unusual
meeting of the Executive Council of Psi Upsilon took
place on February 7th in the Theta Theta Chapter
House at the University of Washington. A cursory
search through the records of the many meetings of
our governing council does not reveal a meeting so
far away from the usual haunts of such gatherings.
The meeting actually covered a
period from the
evening of February 4th to the evening of February
7th and embraced meetings with the Alumru and un
dergraduate Brothers of both the Theta Theta and
the Zeta Zeta at the University of British Columbia. It
took the place of the regular Winter Meeting which

On Friday, February 6th the Executive Council
drove north into the Dominion of Canada to spend
the day with the Alumni and undergraduate Brothers
of the Zeta Zeta at the University of British Columbia.
They were met there by Brother Robert L. Hawkins,
Zeta Zeta '62, who is the only member of the Council
residing in western Canada.
The day was spent with the undergraduate mem
bers of the Zeta Zeta and a small group of Alumni
Brothers who met at the Chapter House for a dis
cussion and determination of a problem of what
should be done with the Chapter House. From the
discussion that preceded a vote it did appear that the
simplest solution was to sell the Chapter House and
find suitable quarters elsewhere for the Chapter. How
ever, the meeting developed a considerable degree of
optimism, where pessimism had prevailed for some
months, and by a considerable majority it was de
termined that it was worth a strenuous effort to keep
the Zeta Zeta in its splendid home.
Another positive result of this foregathering of the
Executive Council and the local Alumni Brothers was
the development of a spirit of determination to pull
together, to develop a more active Alumni Associa
tion and to spend more time with the undergraduates
in the development of more effective rushing pro
grams. It was the general feeUng that both the Theta
Theta and the Zeta Zeta were in situations on their
respective campuses where aggressive, purposeful ap
proaches to rushing would solve whatever problems
have carried over from the wave of "anti-fraterruty
feeling" which plagued all fraternities during the late
sixties and early seventies.
The morning of Friday, February 7th was taken up
witli the return of the motorcade to Seattle for lunch
eon at the Theta Theta and the meeting of the Execu
tive Council which followed. The meeting was at
tended by several Alumni Brothers as well as the
members of the active Chapter. Brother Robert W.
Morey, the President, conducted the meeting in the
true form of a
champion of Psi U. They were seeing
the governing body of Psi Upsilon actually in opera
tion and making its studies of problems manifest to
all.
An interesting sideUght on the meeting, was the
presence of five of the undergraduate Brothers from
tlie Zeta Zeta who, after their meeting with the Coun
cU members in Vancouver, traveled down to Seattle
to be present at this meeting�an
experience that is
rarely shared by many Chapter members, and cer
tainly not before in this area of the country.
The final event of this memorable meeting of the
Council was the "Get-together Cocktail Hour" which
preceded a well planned dinner for aU of those who
had participated in the day's proceedings. Much credit
is due to the Theta Theta Chapter Brothers for tliis
excellent occasion.
Sunday, February 8th was
get-away day for the
members of the Executive Council. Those who had
made the long trek cross-country included Brothers
Robert W. Morey, Henry B. Poor, A. Durston Dodge,
Joseph A. Esquirol, Charles M. HaU, Charles S. P.
Hodge, J. Russell McShane, WiUiam R. Robie, John
Buchanan and Winston Moore.

schedule for about ten days prior to their arrival for
the February 7th meeting. They had visited the Phi,
the Epsilon Nu, and the Iota. They also attended the

Irvine, Cal. and the University of Southern CaUfornia.
The next stop was San Francisco for a meeting of
the Alumni of the Epsilon Chapter (now defunct),
for the purpose of reviewing the prospects of reviving
the Epsilon in the not too distant future. Brothers
Morey and Poor were joined here by Brother Hodge
who flew in from Washington, D.C. to join them.
After the conclusion of a round of meetings and
talks the trio traveled by plane to Seattle for the three
day program which is reported in the accompanying
article.

goodly representation of the active members of the

the oldest social collegiate fraternity in the United

of leading members of several fraternities at Union
CoUege. It was at Union College that Kappa Alpha
was organized by nine students in 1825. The principal
instigator of this gathering was Thomas N. Bonner,
president of Union College.

presented the theme of the meeting as a "manifesto
